boundary_note: Bounded first pass for the frozen Monocacy record (July 9, 1864) in Early's Raid and Operations Against the B&O Railroad [June-August 1864]. The July 7 and 8 skirmishes at Frederick and the July 10 march on Washington are context. Campaign-wide marches, levies, captures, returns and multi-action loss totals are context; they are not assigned to one record or added across records. Draft claims do not alter model inputs.

claims.rationale: No inspected return establishes matched personnel at a common opening boundary. The frozen side-specific numerical strength bounds are blank (missing_numeric_strength). No figure in this pass is adopted as a simultaneous opening force.

claims.value: The frozen force field reads Corps; the live field reads zero. Wallace says Tyler's force by the evening of July 6 was a scant 2,500 men of all arms, besides Clendenin's squadron of 250 and about 200 of the First Potomac Home Brigade; he gives Ricketts's two brigades as 1,750 and 1,600, and says the nine veteran regiments engaged represented 3,350 men. He estimated about 18,000 enemy engaged on the left bank and at least 2,000 more across the river, and later called Early's attacking corps not less than 18,000 while Breckinridge's two divisions stayed in Frederick. Pond gives Wallace 3,350 veterans and 2,500 under Tyler, and Early's army at the start of the march apparently about 17,000. The guns also differ in the accounts: Wallace's six 3-inch rifles against not less than sixteen Napoleons.
claims.rationale: Union figures are unit counts of differing dates; the Confederate figures are Wallace's calculation from the enemy's front and a historian's whole-army estimate from before the march. They are not matched populations. None is adopted as a matched opening strength. The live zero is not measured absence.

claims.value: Wallace says the pikes to Washington and Baltimore and the railroad converge within two miles at the position, that the river covers its entire front with few fords, difficult for artillery, and that the commanding heights are on the eastern bank. Pond says the stream was everywhere fordable, so the position could be turned on either flank. Both say the Confederates crossed at a ford below the Union left.
claims.rationale: Wallace's defensive description and Pond's fordability statement disagree; neither is adjudicated. No map verification. Wallace chose the position during the operation, so it is not tagged inherited.

claims.value: Wallace says he lacked ambulances and wagons, meant to use the railroad cars instead, and that the railroad agent ran away with both his trains; he also says intrenching tools came too late. The three reinforcing regiments halted at Monrovia; Pond says they halted there several hours for rations, six miles from the field, while Wallace calls Monrovia eight miles away. Pond says Early levied $200,000 at Frederick and supplied himself with garments, shoes, bacon and flour.
claims.rationale: Retrospective and interested descriptions, not supply returns; the distance to Monrovia differs between the accounts.

claims.value: Wallace says the invading column's strength, commander and objects were on his part purely conjectural, that reports continued conflicting, and that he fought in part to make the enemy develop his force. Pond says it was still doubtful whether Early aimed at Baltimore or Washington. Wallace also relays a dying Confederate officer's claim that Lee directed the operations in person, adding "give it what weight you please."
claims.rationale: Attributed knowledge from an interested report and a history; no message log inspected.

claims.value: Wallace lists three objects: to keep the rail communication to Harper's Ferry open, to cover the roads to Washington and Baltimore, and to make the enemy develop his force; he says he failed in all but the last. He says his was the only force that could be thrown between the capital and the enemy in time, strong enough to gain time. Pond says Early, too intent on Washington, drew back at sunset.
claims.rationale: Stated aims from an interested report and a history's judgment; the effect on Washington's defence is campaign context, not a tactical measure of this record.

claims.value: Wallace says he chose to fight at the Monocacy, posted Ricketts on the left and Tyler on the right, and ordered Ricketts to retire; he credits Tyler with holding the stone bridge. Pond says Gordon and the cavalry turned the Union left under Breckinridge's direction while Rodes demonstrated. The frozen commanders are Lieutenant General Early and Major General Wallace; the live page gives Early as Major General. No inspected passage describes Early's own orders at the Monocacy.
claims.rationale: Command roles from an interested report and a history; the listed commanders do not receive automatic sole credit, and the live rank is not adopted.

claims.value: The frozen result reads Confederate victory and the live result Confederate Victory. Wallace retreated on the Baltimore pike but says he did not think himself seriously beaten, and that the enemy could not move from the field toward Washington until about noon the next day. NPS calls Monocacy the battle that saved Washington.
claims.rationale: Retain the original result and engagement interval; later movements and campaign contribution are different measures. No new probabilities or individual causal credit. The delay and the Washington claim are campaign contribution, not the tactical result.

claims.value: The frozen casualty text reads 2,359 total; the live field reads 2094 (US 1294; CS 800). Wallace's table gives Ricketts's division 1,649 and a grand total read as 1,968 in OCR; he says over 1,600 of the 3,350 veterans were missing three days after, and in his July 10 telegram that he lost probably not over 200 prisoners. Pond gives 98 killed, 579 wounded and 1,282 missing, total 1,959, notes Early claimed 600 to 700 unwounded prisoners, and gives Early's own killed and wounded as about 700, with 435 wounded found at Frederick; Wallace says over 400 wounded were captured in the Frederick hospital.
claims.rationale: Original casualty returns were not inspected; preserve totals, categories, cutoffs and differences. No canonical reconciliation or casualty-based opening count; related actions must not be added without resolving population overlap. Wallace's table is partly garbled in OCR.

open_questions: Ricketts's report (not found per the compiler), Tyler's, Clendenin's and the regimental reports, Gordon's report, the compiled return No. 7 and Early's July 14 report (selected for DC001, not used here) remain deferred for this record.

NPS/CWSAC is one family. George E. Pond's The Shenandoah Valley in 1864 (Scribner, 1883) is a retrospective history written, by its preface, from the official documents at the War Records Office and field despatches; it quotes the reports of the commanders it describes and is not independent of them. Wallace's July 10 telegram and August 1864 report, printed in Official Records Series I, Volume XXXVII, Part 1, are one family of interested Union accounts. The Official Records volumes are shared containers, not additional witnesses. Report dates are not event times or proof of contemporary knowledge.
No automatic commander attribution, causal campaign score, morale/readiness number or battle/campaign double counting.
